period. I am afraid, too, there is a tendency to forget that the United Nations itself represents a new concept in international affairs. Briefly its purpose, as I see it, is to promote co-operation amongst its members, and along with that to encourage the wealthier nations to help the poorer ones.
I think the house will agree with me that is a relatively new concept in international affairs. The United Nations has created a number of agencies in order to accomplish the purposes I mentioned, among which is the technical assistance organization fund. It is really these agencies, and not the United Nations itself, that do the work for which the United Nations was brought into being. I consider the purpose of the technical assistance fund to be of the greatest importance. I believe the government of Canada should support the fund to the limit of our ability.
I should like to say a brief word about the history of the technical assistance program. It was approved by the general assembly in November, 1949, and was created to meet the great need of the underdeveloped nations for technical aid. It was intended to be a means of implementing economic and social cooperation, a fundamental task of the United Nations as set out in article 55 of the charter. Perhaps the progress made in this endeavour has not been as great as we would have liked. The program probably has not been assisted financially by a number of nations to the extent necessary, and perhaps this is a reason why Canada's aid has not been greater than it has. Whatever the reason may be, my purpose today is to urge that Canada give greater financial support than has been the case in the past.
The program got off to a rather poor start. The amount voted for its work in 1950 only amounted to $20 million. I can recall another $20 million that was voted for a certain purpose in this country. After the general election of 1930, when unemployment was the great issue in Canada, a special session was called to deal with that problem. A sum of $20 million, which at that time was considered to be a large sum of money, was voted to resolve the problems caused by unemployment. Needless to say, the $20 million proved to be totally inadequate for that purpose. When we think of such a sum in relation to the great problems that are facing what we are pleased to call the "underdeveloped countries", we must realize how paltry it is. This $20 million was to cover a period of 18 months, and Canada's contribution was $850,000. If my memory

serves me correctly, about 55 nations contributed, so that was considered to be not too bad a contribution by Canada.
For some reason our contribution in 1952 was reduced by $100,000 and was only $750,000. Probably the reason for that was that the total pledges of all countries was $19 million instead of $20 million. The economic and social council recommended a minimum of $25 million for 1953. Canada again promised to contribute $750,000, with an additional $100,000 on condition that the total of $25 million was contributed. I do not believe that the $25 million was raised, but in any case the Canadian government contributed another $50,000, bringing our total contribution for 1953 up to $800,000.
In my opinion, the expenditure under this heading should not be considered as a charitable handout. It should be considered as a part, and a very important part, of our defence program. I may refer to that again, but if there is one point I wish to get over to the house during the course of my remarks, it is that this contribution to the technical assistance fund should not be considered as a charitable handout, but what it is-that is if we make it of sufficient importance-a material factor in our program for peace. As a matter of fact, I believe government spokesmen at the United Nations agree with me in that contention. I am informed that the requests for economic and technical assistance from needy countries literally poured into United Nations headquarters in 1953, and that because of the lack of adequate financial means a large number of requests could not be met.
It seems strange to me that, although Canada's representative on the economic and social council in 1953 supported recommendations for a general increase in the United Nations budget for technical aid of approximately 31 per cent, Canada offered to increase her own share by only 13 per cent. To indicate how insignificant the total United Nations budget for technical assistance is-I have already made one comparison with the $20 million we voted for unemployment in 1930-I might state that in 1950 the city of New York spent nearly $57 million on garbage removal and street cleaning alone. The total appropriation for technical assistance during any year since the program was launched was considerably less than half of that amount.
In 1949 a committee of experts was set up by the economic and social council to investigate the problem of assisting backward countries. The report of the committee, a 108-page document, was issued in

May 1951. It dealt with the question of development in the underdeveloped countries. How unrealistic is the financial aspect of the United Nations technical program becomes clear as one reads the findings of this report.
The committee estimated that in order to increase by 2 per cent the per capita national incomes in the underdeveloped areas would require an annual capital import well in excess of $10 billion. This report is well worth reading, and if hon. members can get it I am sure they would be well repaid for the time taken to read it. I think copies are difficult to get. I know I borrowed one from the Department of External Affairs.
I shall quote briefly from this report at pages 84 and 86. At page 84 under the heading "Intergovernmental Grants" I find this:
The principle that the better off should help to pay for the education, the medical services and other public services received by the poorer classes of the community is now well established within every member nation of the United Nations. The idea that this principle should also be applied as between rich and poor countries is relatively new.
I emphasize this point, and I think it is something we must keep in mind. It is not only new for the countries that are trying to help, but it is also new for the countries that are being helped. Difficulties may arise there, in addition to the difficulty of finding enough funds from the countries that are helping. It continues:
It has however been put into practice on several occasions. The work of UNRRA is an outstanding example of United Nations collaboration in this sphere.
Then in the paragraph before that-and I read that one first because I felt it should be in that order-the committee of experts has this to say:
We therefore urge most strongly that some mechanism be created by transferring from the developed to the underdeveloped countries, by way of grants-in-aid, a sum of money which should increase rapidly, reaching eventually a level of about $3 billion a year. This would be equivalent to rather less than one per cent of the national incomes of western Europe, Australasia, the United States and Canada.
I imagine that the countries in this group are the ones that provide most of the funds for the purposes of the technical assistance organization. Then the committee goes on to say:
We do not suggest that aid should be given unconditionally to underdeveloped countries. This would not be wise. Each grant should be linked to a specific function, and there should be international verification that the funds are used only for the purpose for which they have been granted.
I think everyone will agree that that is an excellent recommendation.

Then, here are some of the purposes for which the committee of experts indicated the fund could be used:
(a)	Research and education. This includes grants for agricultural extension services, technical schools, farm schools, local universities and for training technicians abroad, grants to departments of governments, research institutes or universities, wherever located, working on problems of underdeveloped countries:
(b)	Public health programs, emphasizing preventive medicine and nutrition rather than curative medicine;
(c)	Subsidization of medium- and short-term farm credit:
(d)	Improvement of rural public works. This includes grants for roads, rural water supplies, land reclamation, drainage, soil conservation, afforestation.
I am sure these are very practical purposes. There is nothing fancy, if I may use that term, in the purposes proposed by the committee of experts.
When the question of establishing a special United Nations fund for economic development was discussed by the economic and social council in October of last year, Canada's representative took the position that Canada was unable at the present time to consider contributing to a development fund, because of the heavy burden of our defence expenditures.
In discussing the proposal, Canada's representative, according to a report in the Montreal Star of October 28, 1953, made this statement:
When sufficient progress has been made in a world-wide scheme of disarmament the Canadian government will undertake to ask the Canadian people to devote any portion of the savings thus achieved to an international fund of the United Nations.
That is to me at least very heartening information. I hope the government means to carry out what its representative asserted on that occasion.
May I say at this point that when I first drafted the resolution to which I am now speaking, it contained another paragraph which I deleted before the resolution reached Votes and Proceedings. That paragraph was pretty much along the same lines as the assertion attributed to Canada's representative at the United Nations, according to the report in the Montreal Star of October 28, 1953.
I believe it was at the same meeting, that of October 28, 1953, the Canadian representative at the United Nations announced that the Canadian government, subject to parliamentary approval, was prepared to increase its contribution to the 1954 expanded program of technical assistance up to a maximum of $1,500,000 U.S. It was stated that this

United Nations
increased contribution would be made if the support for the 1954 program by other countries warranted such action, and if the total of the contributions was sufficient to make a reasonable and workable program.
This may not be an exact quotation, but I took it from the monthly bulletin of the Department of External Affairs for the month of November 1953, at page 323. I regret very much however-the minister may be able to give a reason for it when he speaks-that the item in the estimates for the year 1954 is only $850,000.
As I said, the suggestion made by Canada's representative at the United Nations of increasing the amount that we contribute to technical assistance as soon as the burden of military preparedness is lessened, because of the easing of world tension, is an excellent one, and I do hope, as I know we all do, that the lessening of world tension may enable the government to act on it without delay. I really believe that a start could be made at this session. Indeed I hope-and "hope" is not too strong a word-that the government is not going to renege on that intention.
I hold in my hand the text of a statement made on November 12 by the Canadian representative at the fourth technical assistance conference, and I wish to quote from it because it meets I think in its entirety with my complete approval. It reads:
I am sure that we all agree that the war on want Is the road to peace.
If war on want is the road to peace-and may I say that I agree; I have already indicated that in what I said-then we should consider any contribution under this head not as something to aid people over a difficult period but as something to raise the standard of living of people in less favoured countries than our own, and thus build the sort of atmosphere that makes for peace rather than war.
The statement continues:
The United Nations technical assistance program, by helping to improve standards of living and thus increasing the sense of security and brotherhood among the peoples of the world, is a considerable factor in the building of firm foundations for world peace. In another way, too, it helps in achieving this same purpose. We all know that changes in methods of production, in industrial technology and so on, are likely to hurt someone, even though in the long run the great majority may benefit from them. Our technical assistance program, by providing training and guidance where they may be most needed, can facilitate adjustment to the new ways and reduce to a minimum the temporarily harmful effects of too rapid industrial change. It is of course in the nature of a pilot plant-an experiment, but so far a successful one; . . .
[Mr. Maclnnis.j
May I interject here that this has been in my opinion so successful that we should not hesitate to increase our contribution to it. The statement goes on:
-successful not least because all countries can contribute something useful to others. In fact, and from a selfish point of view, though we do not expect to be the direct recipient of technical assistance ourselves, we are sure that we, like others, shall share in the benefits of the program as a whole.
I said I was reading this because it is an excellent statement which every hon. member can approve. Before this debate on the resolution concludes I hope we shall have an expression of opinion, if not by a vote, at least by word of mouth, from those who are supporting the resolution that we do believe in this approach to this very important problem.

I rise
to give my unqualified support to the resolution just introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis). I do so because I have had some experience in underdeveloped countries, and I can testify to the value of this particular program. In my opinion the resolution suggests a form of assistance to underdeveloped countries, particularly those in the Far East or the Asian countries, which far exceeds in effectiveness any other proposal that has ever been made.
It must be remembered that while I support this suggestion, that Canada should be generous in the amounts set aside for this particular program, she is already, in company with many other countries of the commonwealth and indeed other members of the United Nations Organization, contributing and doing much in this field. One has only to learn something of the work of such organizations or agencies as UNESCO, the world health organization, UNICEF, the international labour organization and many other agencies. All of them have done work of this kind to improve the conditions of those people who live in countries which we are describing as underdeveloped. It must be realized, too, that all of them are based upon the fundamental concept that the best form of assistance is that which helps a person or a country to stand upon its own feet, and to stimulate a desire for self-development and improvement, to the end that self-support and independence may be the final result.
It is important, too, to understand that no self-respecting nation wishes to be the spasmodic or even the constant recipient of gifts in the form of charity. It does not matter in what form those gifts may be made, unless there is a program which will stimulate the

self-development of those people, then it fails just by that much. There is in all these countries the hunger for that kind of help which does no violence to individual or national pride.
It is well known that throughout all those "have not" countries there is a stirring of national consciousness and pride. This is desirable because it is accompanied by a desire to improve standards of living, which can only come about under two conditions, in my opinion: One, the absence of war and rumours of war; two, by receiving advice from those countries better developed, and continuing to give technical assistance so that the industries and resources of those countries may be developed by the use, or the implementation of suggestions leading to the use, of better techniques.
I would assert, Mr. Speaker, in fact, I know from actual experience, that assistance of the kind anticipated by this resolution is the only kind likely to achieve the thing we have in view, namely, the lifting up of our unfortunate brethren to a fuller and more satisfying life. I think Canada is especially placed in this regard and in a position to take the lead in this respect. I say frankly, and once again from actual experience, that there is no suspicion of ulterior motives attached to the name "Canada". In this we are unique. No matter how much they do or for how long other countries have been participating in these programs, there has always been a suspicion in the minds of some people: "What is the aim of this system?" No such suspicion attaches to Canada. That is why I think we are in a favoured position. We can move along and do what we can to help these people. Our ultimate objective is not questioned.
It was my good fortune in 1950-51 to represent Canada as a member of a three-man educational mission to Burma, one of the Asian countries. I spent six months in that delightful country travelling from north to south and from east to west. Our mission was educational in character. We were to investigate all aspects of the educational system of that country and make such recommendations as we thought proper for its improvement.
My own particular assignment had to do with the subject matter of the resolution which we have before us; it was in the field of technical and vocational education. It was my good fortune to see something of the conditions in India, Pakistan and Thailand from brief visits. I was also able to consult with scores of people representing varied groups, all with the same object in view- giving technical advice of one kind or 83276-124J

another and assisting in various ways. I mention this trip of mine only to support my views as being based upon experience. In other words, I think I know what I am talking about and that is useful.
And unusual.

Burma is typical of other countries in that part of the world. It is a potentially rich country with most delightful people. But they are badly educated; they are wrongly educated in that their education has not fitted them to develop their own resources and to make their contribution where they live. Here we have a people with a national consciousness who feel constantly that they want to run their own show but who are frustrated because they feel unable to do it. They are rich in resources but poor in their ability to develop those resources.
I stated earlier that in my opinion the best form of assistance is one in which we take the long view. By hastening slowly we can put these people in a position, by training and education and guidance and help, to develop their own resources and to exploit them for themselves. Thus and thus only they may be able to raise their standards of living and contribute to the progress of society.
Of course the first thing they want is peace, because it is only under a condition of peace that they can obtain those skills which we hope to impart to them. You hear the cry throughout the Far East, India for the Indians, Burma for the Burmese, and so on. They do not want gifts from above unless they are given with the distinct understanding that the country is to be developed by its own people.
In my opinion it is useless to send out technicians and engineers unless they are going to institute a training program to train the people in those countries to become engineers and technicians. How can I do otherwise than urge a more generous attitude on the part of my own country when I have made certain recommendations in connection with Burma? I should like to quote some of the recommendations which I made. They are as follows;
1.	That a director of technical education be appointed to serve in the department of education. That he be responsible for the over-all organization and direction of all forms of practical education.
2.	That an advisory board of leaders in industry and engineering be appointed to act in a consultative capacity on technical education.
3.	That at least two officials be appointed to plan and supervise actual instruction and to organize and conduct instructor-training courses.

Perhaps I might develop one or two of those recommendations, particularly the one with respect to cottage industries. May I presume to explain to the house the conditions under -which the people live in countries such as I am describing. This is an agricultural country, as most of them are, with a one-crop economy, that of rice. Between the harvesting of the crop and the planting of the new crop there is a long period of time. In most villages the people engage in cottage industries. That is to say, in their own homes they make a variety of articles. They weave silk, they make articles of apparel, ornaments and tools of various kinds.
If I may digress for a moment, I found boys and men making with very crude tools, cigarette lighters which they sold for seven rupees or $1.50 per dozen. They do very nice work in all these cottage industries; in fact they do marvellous work, but their tools are very crude and their output is limited. In other words, these people are living under substandard conditions. It is most certain they could increase their production and the saleability of their goods if they had proper instruction in more modern techniques, and particularly if they could be supplied with the proper tools and equipment. That is why one of the recommendations was that mobile units go around to give proper instruction. We felt, and I used this expression before, that we should make haste slowly.
That brings me to another point in connection with finance. I have supported the idea that Canada and other countries should be more generous in the provision of financial help to increase the ability of these people to develop their own resources. But I submit that it is not only the voting of money that will be effective. You can use only so much money at a time. We should vote sufficient money to initiate a program capable of being carried out and gradually increase it as we go along.

If I may summarize what I have said, Mr. Speaker, I would say, in conclusion, that there is a great need. There is no doubt about that. We have vast numbers of people living in conditions under which we could not survive. They are ignorant of modern methods in regard to almost anything you could mention.
I was particularly struck with the efficiency and valuable work done in this regard by the world health organization. When you see the conditions under which so many people live and eat, you are appalled that any of them are alive. I am thinking of one country in particular where the infant mortality rate is 50 per cent up to the age of 10, and that I believe is due to the fact that they are absolutely ignorant of any notion of sanitation, food preparation, food care, child care, and care of expectant mothers.
In my opinion the best organization we have in the whole gamut of world organizations is the world health organization, because unless people are living healthy lives you cannot do much for them. However, here we have a need and an urge from the people themselves. They want to develop their own country themselves. They want to be shown how to do it and then left alone. They do not want someone dominating them and telling them, "This is the way we do it in Canada and therefore you must do it in this way." In assisting these people we should recruit the type of person who understands them, their desires and aspirations and who will help them to build themselves up. It will be a slow process.
These people have a desire for peaceful development in order to become self-supporting. They have inadequate finances. In the country which I have described, the national budget was U.S. dollars $118 million, and they have an army, a navy and an air force. Perhaps I should complete the picture by stating that the total population is about 18 million people.
So far as Canada and the other western nations are concerned, it is essential that these people be persuaded that we have the very best of intentions. There is no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, that to a program of this kind, while it has all the qualities we attach to it, among them being the idea of helping our fallen or underprivileged brethren, there attaches another practical and unquestionable value. It is no good talking to people who have very little to eat and ask them to choose between democracy and communism. They do not care two pins about that. They do not understand what

we are talking about. The thing to do is to show them by example and precept that we are interested in them and that our way of life is the better way of life.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, what do we get out of it as a nation? I believe we get the satisfaction of doing with our abundance something which will help those in poorer circumstances. That is about all. But we will make friends and surely this is an opportunity not to be neglected.

Mr. Speaker, I want to give all the support I can to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), except in regard to one or two small details. I cannot agree with his split infinitive because I do not think that would get by my editor. Apart from that I am 100 per cent in accord with this resolution, which calls for a substantial increase in the technical assistance grant.
I believe it is typical of this government that when the question first arose at the United Nations last fall, and when there was some suggestion that some of the other countries might cut down their grants for technical assistance, many people in Canada, solidly behind the United Nations, began to get nervous and make inquiries of the government, and one of the clearest-cut answers we ever got about extra spending of money by the government was that perhaps there would be extra funds forthcoming for this purpose.
I myself, Mr. Speaker, have written quite a few letters to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on various subjects, each suggesting that perhaps a little more money could be spent on this or that, and it was like trying to get blood out of a stone. But at least we did get a little blood out of the stone in this particular respect.
Seriously speaking, though, I believe this is one of the most important matters to come before the house and before our whole generation. In connection with my own duties as a newspaper writer over the past few years I have had the great privilege and responsibility of travelling a good deal in many of the countries with which these technical assistance grants are chiefly concerned, namely those countries along the northern shores of Africa, that part of the world we call the Middle East, and out into Pakistan, India, Ceylon, and so on.
I came home from these trips, Mr. Speaker, convinced that we are living at a great turning point in history, and at the end of that three or four hundred year period of history which we know as the age of the white man's rule; although why anyone should refer to
United Nations
us, dirty greys or pale pinks, as whites I have never been able to figure out. However, the historical age of the white man's domination has come to an end. Those particular circumstances which existed for three or four hundred years, and under which the part of the human race which we represent happened to have a supremacy over the rest of the human family, which it never had before and will never have again, have gone. The great and fundamental question of our time is how the transition is going to be made from the age of white man's supremacy to the age of partnership and equality between all the great racial sections of the human family.
There was one minor point, perhaps of emphasis, which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway made and with which I would slightly disagree, to this extent, that we' should consider this, as I understood him to>
say, as part of our national defence.
I believe we have to be very careful when we begin to think of technical assistance grants in terms of our national defence. In my opinion, in countries such as India there is one thing they are afraid of more than anything else, and that is that organized benevolence from western countries is tied up with some ulterior purpose such as defence. I believe one of the terribly unfortunate consequences, for example, of the attempt to establish American bases in Pakistan and its repercussion in India arose more from that simple fact, because the nations of Asia are fearful that there may be ulterior motives in these great humanitarian purposes.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, when I came home from these crucial parts of the world I came home with the belief that we are at a great turning point in history. In countries such as, say, Egypt, or the Arab states, or any of these Moslem countries

what might be called the whole brown belt of the earth-you see these depressed and ignorant people just pushing up as it were through a thin shell, and one can see that they are determined to have a larger share of the good things of life. Surely we have a great opportunity to give them that in a new guise. As far as I could see, nothing in that part of the world has so changed the opinion of the peoples of those countries and helped to dissipate their suspicions. I would say that the greatest contribution there has ever been to a better understanding between Asia and the west is our own Colombo plan, and I would certainly hope that either in this debate or on an early occasion the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) would report on his inspection of the Colombo plan projects, because I have heard him speak on it and it is one of the

United Nations
finest speeches I have heard, so far as a firsthand account of what the Colombo plan means is concerned.
I think, however, there is a very real point implied in the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), that we should be extremely careful not to suggest to the people of these backward or so-called underdeveloped countries that we are holding out a helping hand to them only to keep them alive long enough so that they may be able to fight on our side in some future war with Soviet Russia. I think there is a very real and vital purpose involved and that we have a very real basis of self-interest in making sure that these great undecided countries of that crucial part of the world do receive effective assistance from the West in .time.
I travelled through many of the countries that our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is going to visit, and I came home from the East convinced that the peoples of these undecided countries in Africa, the Middle East and South Asia are not so ignorant that they do not realize the situation. All of them are looking to the two greatest and most populous nations of the East. The most populous nation, and potentially the greatest nation on earth, is of course China, which has gone communist. The second most populous country in the world is India, which is trying to adapt western democracy to that Asian soil. To my mind the most heartening and gigantic landmark of that area, of such great promise for the future of democracy, lies in the fact that that country, which had never known any democracy and where only a tiny fraction of the people know how to read and write, could stage its great national election and render a verdict with just as much intelligence and orderliness as has ever been rendered in our own mature democracies of the West.
That is a lesson to us. But make no mistake that all of the undecided peoples of the earth in Africa, the Middle East and South Asia are looking to the two great nations of the East. One of those nations has gone communist. One of them is trying to adapt our western form of democracy and make it survive and thrive in that Asian soil. Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker. If what is called totalitarianism, with all its suppression of freedoms and the brutal shortcuts that it takes, can deliver for the great mass of these people a better standard of living than is provided over a period of years in India, which is trying to use our western techniques and our voluntary system, then regardless of anything we say here or that is said anywhere else it is my opinion that the balance of world
[Mr. Philpott.l
power is not going to fall on the side of democracy but on the side of totalitarian communism. In my opinion that would be a tragedy not only for the great undecided parts of the earth but for us.
I am heartily in accord with all the technical and similar assistance that we can promote. Finally, I would interpret the term "technical assistance" in the widest possible manner. If I were in a position of any power I would not only be sending out engineers to build big water power dams and so on, but even to both sides of the iron curtain I would be sending those who for example practise the art practised by Barbara Ann Scott in order to demonstrate to these people some of the arts, sciences and amenities of our western world. In other words, I would interpret the term in the widest possible sense in order to send to all corners of the world, but primarily to our own potential friends, all of the good things from this western land with which we can help them.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise to give my wholehearted support to the resolution in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis). I do so because of the experience I had when with the Canadian delegation to the United Nations in New York last fall. I was struck by the fact that the most successful of all works carried out by the United Nations were in the social field, and more particularly in the field of aid to underdeveloped countries. As we all know, the United Nations does not legislate. It simply recommends, and it is only to the extent to which the member countries will cooperate that the work of the United Nations can be successful.
I found that in the field of assistance to underdeveloped countries the United Nations was accomplishing something concrete, that there was something going out of the United Nations which carried weight. On the other hand, I am afraid that many other branches of the work of the United Nations are not nearly as successful. So far as aid to underdeveloped countries is concerned, I think the most important field is that of technical assistance. As often as I could I attended the meetings of the committee which was dealing with this matter. I was there when all the countries were making their pledges, and I thought that the technical assistance organization was making a marvellous contribution towards the welfare of the world as a whole. I am glad to say that I am not the only one who holds that opinion. In the booklet,

"Canada and the United Nations 1952-53", published by the Department of External Affairs, I find the following on page 30:
The most notable achievement of the United Nations in this field-
The reference is to the social field.
-has been in the provision of technical experts, training and demonstration equipment to the underdeveloped countries.
I might give a few more figures from this report in addition to those already given by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way. I continue:
In 1950 the expanded program of technical assistance was undertaken, to finance which 55 countries pledged the equivalent of $20,070,260 for an eighteen-month period ending December 31, 1951.
For the second period of twelve months $18,795,355 was pledged by 65 countries, and for the third period (1953) 67 governments pledged $21,278,575. Canadian contributions for each of these periods were $772,727, $750,000, and $800,000 respectively. Within the framework of the Colombo plan, Canada has also made available $400,000 each year over the past three years for technical assistance to south and southeast Asia.
I will be the first, Mr. Speaker, to say that the Canadian contribution to the United Nations for technical assistance and to the Colombo plan is to be commended. I am of the opinion, however, that it is not enough. If we look at the populations of the various countries, perhaps we can say we are doing a good job. We must consider more than the population and the size of the countries, however; we must consider the capabilities and natural wealth of the countries. If we take that into consideration, Canada is one of the wealthiest countries, and has probably about the highest potential of any country in the world. These facts have to be considered when we think about the amount of the contribution we must make to the various international organizations.
As hon. members know, the various countries, many of them not United Nations countries, gather together and pledge so much money towards the work of the technical assistance organization. This money is then spent in sending specialists, scientists and technicians into the various needy countries to discuss production problems and difficulties. I might say that these problems relate not only to production, or any one field of production, but cover communications, highway projects and so on. I feel that this is extremely important in that it does not give direct relief to these countries. It does make them more self-sufficient by giving them the knowledge to extend their own production and make them more and more self-sufficient.
United Nations
It gives them a greater feeling of national pride and a greater incentive to go ahead on their own.
We have found that the greatest hardships occur, as we would expect, in the most densely populated countries. Almost invariably these countries are backward in their production methods. This fact, coupled with the dense population, makes it practically impossible for them to maintain any worthwhile standard of living. We want to assist them to increase their production to the point where they can at least give the people within the country something to eat. We are making a great success of that.
There is one point, however, about which possibly the minister might make some sort of recommendation. I know that during 1953 many of the countries made pledges but contributed not one cent towards the fund. I do not know how many years that has occurred, but I can recall at least two or three countries which did not fulfil their pledge. I shall not name them in this house. This situation adds considerable weight to the burden on the shoulders of those countries that are living up to their pledges. I do not know whether the minister can give us any indication of how much of the money or assistance goes behind the iron or bamboo curtains. I am a little bit concerned about that.
I do not want the people of the communist-dominated countries to have too poor a standard of living, nor do I want them to be refused any assistance. The very terms of the Russian pledge make me ask this question. When the Russian delegate made his pledge, I think it was $2 million for the coming year, he attached a condition that this money was not to pass through the hands of the organization but was to be spent within the communist countries. In other words, the Russian pledge amounted to no pledge at all. The Russians agreed to give assistance to their own communist people, but no aid whatever to any other country. I believe the conditions attached to that pledge are a good indication of the Russian attitude throughout the United Nations. During the time I was at the United Nations I could not find any indication of a co-operative spirit on the part of Russia or its satellites. In every committee and in the general assembly, their speeches followed exactly the same lines. The Russian delegate made a speech and the satellites followed one after the other making practically the same speech.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I was told, somewhat in jest, that when anything comes up in the United Nations to be discussed

United Nations
either in committee or before the general assembly, the Russian research people are told to write six speeches on that particular subject. Then, the Russian delegate chooses the best one and hands out the rest of them to the satellite delegates. I do not know how much truth there is in that. As I said a moment ago, it is not only Canada's contribution that is insufficient, but the total contribution to the technical assistance organization is insufficient. I find that the Secretary General of the United Nations agrees with me wholeheartedly.
In his annual report on the work of the United Nations from July, 1952, to the end of June, 1953, he says on page 95:
It may be that in comparative terms, the program-
That is the technical assistance program.
__is a modest one. It may be that the total amount
of assistance it has been able to render is, in relation to the needs of the underdeveloped countries, pitiably small. But whatever its scale, it is now a co-operative venture that has great appeal and motive power . . .
The indication is that the amount of assistance given under the program is pitiably small when compared to the need throughout the world. I would urge that Canada, with the wealth we have, lead the way in getting the contributing countries to build up their contributions in order to give these underdeveloped countries at least a small amount of security, and thus enable them to avoid falling into communist slavery.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secreiary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to take part in the discussion of this resolution; and I am also grateful, as I am sure the house is, to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) for making that possible.
After all, this resolution deals with a subject the long-range importance of which may well be very great indeed for international co-operation, and indeed for international peace. Because, though history does not prove that a nation consisting of people with full stomachs is necessarily a peaceful nation, certainly history does prove that a nation consisting of people with empty stomachs will be a troublesome one.
This purpose of United Nations technical assistance is to improve material conditions in what, sometimes a little glibly, we call the underdeveloped countries of the world. I always like to use the expression "materially underdeveloped" when referring to these countries because, in some ways, they are quite as highly developed as we are.
I agree wholeheartedly with the thoughtful and constructive speeches which have been
IMr. Thomas.]
made by those who have spoken in the debate, especially in the importance that has been attached by the speakers to the problems and possibilities presented to us, in the western world-that west which, as Professor Toynbee has reminded us, is now surrounded by the world. These problems are particularly affected by the emerging importance of Asia into the new world of industry, and of technique, of the atom and the jet.
At the United Nations we are often reminded by Asian and African speakers that Asia and Africa are on the march, and that they will not be stopped. That of course is true; and there is no reason why we should want to stop them. But we should of course do our best to assist that march toward peaceful co-operation and free progress. And the kind of work referred to in the resolution is one way in which we can help direct that march in the right direction. That is why the subject is such an important one.
In its terms, the resolution is restricted to the United Nations technical assistance organization, and suggests that the government-
-should consider the advisability of introducing legislation at this session to substantially increase Canada's contribution to the United Nations technical assistance organization fund.
I do not myself mind the split infinitive particularly.
I would hope, in view of what I will be able to say about our contribution to that work, that it may not be necessary to divide the house on a matter concerning which I think there is such substantial and, indeed, unanimous agreement.
In the first place, we must make clear the distinction between relief, economic development, and technical assistance itself. So far as relief is concerned-and that is not mentioned in this resolution-the United Nations of course is doing important work in this field, especially at the present time in Korea, where Canada has I think played a respectable part.
Then, also, if you like, under that broad category of relief you might consider our contribution to the UN children's fund. We have also made a worth-while contribution to that.
Then there is economic development, which of course is something beyond and apart from technical assistance, and which consists of making loans through international agencies, or through a national agency, and making available credits and investment funds to other countries to help them in their capital and economic development.

The first international agency which comes to mind in that field of course is the international bank. Canada has made available to the international bank, for purposes I have just indicated-lending and re-lending-the whole of her original dollar subscription to the bank's capital, amounting to some $58 million. That is the largest subscription for this purpose of any member of the bank, except the United States. Up to this point the bank itself has advanced by way of loans and credits somewhat over $1,700 million. So something is being done through international agencies in that field.
Then there is technical assistance proper, which is the subject of the resolution before us. There are of course two kinds of technical assistance. There is technical assistance w'hich is worked out bilaterally between the contributing government and the receiving government. There comes to mind in this connection the United States point four program, and our own commonwealth Colombo plan under which contributing governments work out plans bilaterally with the receiving government. I am sure my colleague the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) will be able to give information on this. I believe this plan is now working very satisfactorily.
Canada has contributed in the first three years of the Colombo plan something over $75 million for capital assistance and over $1 million for technical assistance. And this year the government will ask parliament to vote $25,400,000-I believe that is the amount tentatively agreed upon-of which a portion will be for technical assistance proper.
Then there are the multilateral schemes for technical assistance, one of which is referred to in the resolution before us. United Nations schemes for technical assistance can, in their turn, be divided first into the ordinary United Nations program, which comes out of the annual budget of the United Nations, and the budgets of the various specialized agencies, through which Canada has already made a pretty respectable contribution in terms of money and in terms of men. And second, there is the scheme which I think the author of the resolution has particularly in mind, that known as the United Nations expanded program for technical assistance.
That program, and the other United Nations program, is carefully organized and controlled by various international bodies. There is, first, the technical assistance committee, under the economic and social council, which represents the 18 governments on the council. It has a sort of general supervisory jurisdiction over all United Nations schemes of this kind. And then there is the technical assistance administration, the administrating body of
United Nations
the secretariat, which looks after particular schemes, and which now is presided over by a distinguished Canadian, Dr. Keenleyside, who has served in our external affairs service. And, finally, there is the technical assistance board, which includes representatives of the various specialized agencies, and which meets periodically to co-ordinate the work done by these various agencies and by outside agencies in order to keep overlapping and duplication to a minimum.
That is a very important function; because, as hon. members know, it is very easy in schemes of this kind, especially internationally organized and administered schemes, to duplicate and to overlap. It is very important that the various programs should be balanced, that they should be co-ordinated under wise central direction, and that business judgment should be used to the maximum extent possible in their implementation.
One thing of course that has to be determined by the supervising agencies-and this is also of importance-is the absorptive capacity of a country for technical assistance or for economic aid, so that money will not be poured into a country that cannot be productively used for particular projects, and that the applications of the various governments for help and for funds are carefully scrutinized. As Professor Frank Scott of Montreal, who was concerned with a particular technical assistance program of the United Nations in Burma, has reminded us in a pamphlet "World War Against Poverty", published by the Royal Society of Canada, it is customary for governments, being human, to ask for more than they can usefully spend in a limited time. All these things have to be considered before work can start, or else the work will not be done as effectively as it should be.
Now it is true, and it has been pointed out by previous speakers, that while this may be one of the most important aspects of United Nations work, it is not a phase of that work which gets very much publicity or very many headlines, and that is unfortunate. Too often do we interpret the United Nations in terms of political controversy and not in terms of constructive social and economic activity. It is true and it is too bad that conflicts and controversy are their own publicity agents, but very constructive, quiet social and economic work has no one to sing its praise. Those of us who have been at the United Nations know from experience that if there is a speech by Mr. Vishinsky, which is bound to be controversial, or if there is a discussion of the admission of communist China to the United Nations, the galleries will be filled, the delegates' seats will be filled, the television cameras will all be running and the

United Nations
headlines will appear the next day in bold form. But a meeting which may have been held in a committee room in the same building to discuss how to increase food production or eradicate malaria in some Asian or African country will not, I fear, get very much attention or very much publicity. Nonetheless this is important work and we should, I think, be proud to make our contribution to it, as we in this country are doing.
This kind of international technical assistance work and economic aid suffers from two weaknesses, or at least it gets opposition from two sides. There are those who are cynical about it, who are un-co-operative, who do not believe in throwing our money around in foreign countries for what they would call international charity-though it is not charity-and who react in the wrong way to schemes of this kind, the advantage of which is very often long-range rather than immediate. But this work sometimes suffers also from a surfeit of sentimentality and a shortage of practicality on the part of those who would pour funds into projects which would do no good to the people whom they are meant to assist, and might under certain circumstances even do them harm.
There is a danger in this field of attempting to do too much in the wrong way, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. Fairey); to do it our way because it is our way, not because it is necessarily the right way. Those dangers have been emphasized in a very useful and interesting publication which has been printed under the auspices of UNESCO and edited by Dr. Margaret Mead of New York, called "Cultural Patterns and Technical Change". She has this to say about the wrong approach to technical assistance:
To introduce change effectively, it is necessary to know existing conditions. Where it involves implementation by people, it must first be accepted. Otherwise the new proposals, however simple, will be defeated. When pest control is imperative, people will nevertheless release the rats from their traps. Where immunization of cattle is necessary farmers will hide their cattle. And where land reform is introduced without accompanying measures for a reform credit system, the land will again be concentrated in the hands of a few within a few years. And since change is proposed in the interests of human welfare, it is important to see to it that it is introduced constructively or, at any rate, with a minimum of disruption and destruction of established inter-relationships and values. Basic attitudes, concepts, and values are, therefore, here considered.
Then she quotes some very interesting examples of what follows when these right

principles are not applied to technical assistance and aid. I again read from her publication:
In Burma, deep ploughing introduced by European agricultural experts broke up the hard pan that held the water in the rice fields. The weeding of rubber plantations reduced the sap. The new tomato, which the Burmese were persuaded to grow (by technical assistance experts) because it was more productive, had a flavour they did not like, (and they would not eat it). In Turkey, experts trained abroad persuaded some of the younger peasants to remove the stones from their tilled land; when the grain sprouted, the fields of the old men had a better crop, since, in that dry climate, the stones served the function of preserving moisture. In Greece, the wheat in fertilized fields did not resist the drought as well as the wheat in other fields, and the experts realized that earlier-ripening varieties should be planted if the fields were to be fertilized. Mistakes of this sort are acceptable to people who are willing to take the risk of trying the new; but they shake the faith of those who believe in tried and proven procedure alone.
Therefore, as we all agree, it is not only necessary to have the resources to do this work; it is necessary that the work should be done in the right way and on the right principles. In that connection the principles that should underlie technical assistance work were very well and impressively outlined the other day in Washington by the director of the foreign operations administration of the United States, Mr. Harold E. Stassen, when he said-and this has also been emphasized by speakers in this debate-we should not consider this activity as a form of handout or charity. Mr. Stassen said:
Technical assistance is not a "give-away" program. To conduct it as such would be the quickest way to destroy it. Projects undertaken should therefore be co-operative in nature and every single program and project must be based on a careful study of local needs, local conditions, local resources available and desires of the host governments.
The aim of such programs is not to subsidize, not to bolster weak spots, but to lay foundations for self-improvement through work on the elimination of debilitating diseases and the control of conditions endangering health and life; through dissemination of knowledge regarding better farm methods; through the improvement of education; through providing technical advice on matters of transportation to enable people to bring the product of their toil to market, and to break the insulation of mind and body in which so many still live.
When these right principles are applied to practical projects the experience of the United Nations already-and it is a short experience -shows that some astonishingly productive results can be achieved from small expenditures and very small changes.
A year or two ago the United Nations sent a technical assistance mission to Afghanistan. In that mission were technical experts from 14 countries covering an extensive range of

skills. They were sent to help the Afghan people move toward economic and social betterment. The mission included a public administrator from France, a geologist and a nurse from the Netherlands, a plant entomologist from the United Kingdom, a sericul-turalist from China, a Polish statistician, a Danish pediatrician, experts in teacher training and agricultural development from the United States, a public health adviser from India, and a Finnish obstetrician. I suppose obstetrics could be considered a form of technical assistance.
Very much so.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
One simple and inexpensive change was introduced into Afghanistan by Mr. John Dickenson, a farmer from Arkansas, who obtained great results by introducing the hitherto unheard-of common hoe. Mr. Owen, who is in charge of the UN technical assistance board, reported on this as follows:
Traditionally the Afghan farmers have broadcast their cotton seed like wheat. But our agricultural expert proved, on his 34 demonstration plots, that if the cotton is planted in rows and if the farmer will use the hoe instead of the heavy mattock, then production will improve. In fact the first demonstration produced a yield two-and-a-half times greater than by the traditional methods, and the government promptly ordered 30,000 hoes, as well as encouraging their manufacture by local blacksmiths. By such very simple, indeed almost primitive, means as these, a small but decisive revolution is being brought about in Afghan production.
In addition to this kind of technical help, as has been pointed out already today, these people need sympathy, understanding and a knowledge of their local customs. In some respects that kind of approach and that kind of understanding are just as important as material support. Having said that, I should add that material support must follow sympathy and understanding or they cannot be effectively used. Perhaps for a moment we might look at what has been contributed by the United Nations in the way of material support.
I know that the amount has been put on the record already, and I know also that it is small indeed in terms of the astronomical figure devoted to armaments. It is also small indeed in terms of the need and necessity of these people, but it is not quite so small in terms of the practical results which can be accomplished in the early stages of this new international work. We have already had proof of that in our experience with the Colombo plan. I do not think it is wrong to say that if we had contributed twice as much to the Colombo plan in the first two years we would not have been able to effectively spend that total amount.
United Nations
Having regard to those circumstances, the record shows that in the first 18 months of the expanded program of technical assistance a total of $20,070,000 was contributed by members of the United Nations. Canada contributed $850,000. In 1952 the total was $19,000,000, and our contribution was $750,000. In 1953 the total amount went up to $22,000,000 while our contribution went up to $800,000. We have been trying to keep what we think is a fair relationship between our contribution and the total amount contributed by the United Nations. While what we contribute should not necessarily be determined by what others contribute, nevertheless that is a factor which has to be taken into consideration, even if it is not the overriding consideration.
In the current year 1954, according to the latest information which we have been able to secure, and it is as of yesterday, 70 countries, partly as the result of an intensive campaign which has been put on in New York, have pledged themselves to contribute to the technical assistance fund. The amount firmly pledged is something over $24 million.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) has asked whether we could not do something ourselves to ensure that these pledges are converted into payments. We have through our delegation to the United Nations played a very active part in trying to have the pledges increased. In fact in 1952 my colleague the Minister of Northern Development and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) was the chairman of the pledging committee. We also played a most active part in the pledging committee last autumn. We did what we could to get the amount up, and as an earnest of our endeavour in that regard we indicated through our representative to the United Nations, Senator McKeen, that we would increase our amount this year from $800,000 to $1,500,000. That is, we would ask parliament to increase the amount provided the support from other contributors warranted such an amount, and provided the total amount pledged was such as to keep the program at an economically sound level.
We made that offer last autumn, which represented a considerable proportionate increase, and I think it had something to do with the other countries increasing their amounts. At least I hope it had. As a result there has been pledged already this year some $24 million. It seems clear that the conditions which we have laid down in regard to the increase in our contribution are to be fulfilled, and therefore it will be the intention of the government when that is confirmed to

United Nations
include an amount of $700,000 in the supplementary estimates to bring our total contribution to this program up to $1,500,000.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin asked in his speech whether I could give any information as to the expenditures from this fund behind the iron and bamboo curtains. So far as I know, and I think I have the facts, no United Nations funds contributed to the expanded program of technical assistance have been expended in those countries to which the hon. member referred. Of course they have their own schemes for technical assistance. We do get information, for instance, of Soviet help in the way of technical assistance programs in China, but that is quite apart from the United Nations program.
As was indicated, last autumn the Soviet representative made a pledge of approximately $1 million to the United Nations scheme for the current year 1953 but, as pointed out, that pledge was hedged around with certain conditions which were not satisfactory to the United Nations technical assistance administration because they violated the principles which govern technical assistance and which were laid down by the economic and social council. However, that matter is being taken up with the Soviet government by the United Nations officials in charge of this activity, and it is hoped that those conditions will be withdrawn so that this amount can be used in the way in which it should be used, without strings attached.
The Canadian contribution to technical assistance has been exceeded only by that of the United Kingdom, the United States and France in the past. If parliament votes the amount which probably will be requested this year in the main and supplementary estimates, Canada's contribution will be the third largest of the members of the United Nations. I do not think that is anything we should say boastfully, but it does at least show we are playing a respectable part in this very important effort.
We are also playing a part not only in the contribution of funds but in the contribution of experts through the United Nations. In Canada today there are 217 United Nations technical assistance trainees out of a total of 300; the rest of them come under the Colombo plan program. And there are 96 Canadian experts now serving abroad in the United Nations.
Under the Colombo plan program it has been difficult to find as many qualified people as we have been asked to provide and as we would have liked to provide because experts of the kind required are in

great demand in this country. Some of them have had to make considerable sacrifices to take part in this important UN work. The training of experts, in the last analysis, is just about as important as supplying capital assistance, because eventually this kind of work has to be done by these people in their own countries. When we can get them to come here and learn our technical methods and send them back to do the work themselves, that is the kind of help that really matters.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my agreement with the spirit and indeed the content of this resolution, and to emphasize that we are doing something to carry out the advice contained in it. I also express the hope that it will commend itself to all hon. members in this house because, as has been said more than once, the war on want and backwardness, on deprivation and distress, is a road to peace.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief comments on this matter. It is, of course, terribly difficult to really arouse much interest in this chamber in matters on which we all agree. I do not know whether it is because we have a lurking suspicion that when we agree with those we have found to be wrong so often we ourselves must be wrong in agreeing; but whatever the reason, it is always difficult to arouse the kind of interest there should be.
Speaking seriously, I suppose it is obvious that when we do agree on something we have a fair chance of being right. I feel it is a pity that we get so used to living in a world of tension, a dangerous world that we inevitably have to take in our stride. In discussing a matter such as this this afternoon we are really facing a fact that we are in a world where there is a battle going on for men's minds. That sounds easy to say, but it does not really carry much conviction with anyone because we have heard it so often. But it is very true that as well as the material defences of NATO on which we spend so much and from which we hope for so much this battle for men's minds is going on and that in the long run the success or failure of our civilization is going to depend on who wins this battle.
If we look back even a few decades to our relationship with the rest of the world, or at any rate the Asian world which is now coming to bulk so enormously in international affairs, we realize that our contact with these nations was almost wholly through soldiers and missionaries. The next contact, I think it will be agreed, was through physicians. The missionaries began

to find they really had to have a medical training in order to do their best work. Finally we begain to realize that the whole relationship had a material aspect, and that the have-not nations were not going to go on forever quite content to be infinitely worse off than the rest of us.
In the last few years this attitude of acquiescence, which I imagine used to amaze us because it lasted so long, has largely disappeared. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was wise in the remark he made when he left Ottawa, when he described his visit to those countries in Asia which used to be just a romantic concept over the horizon. The Prime Minister said, among other things, "We will not get anywhere unless we treat them as equals".
I want to refer for just a moment to what I might call our legalistic relationship with the nations of Asia by reason of a covenant in the United Nations charter to which we are a party. I want to read articles 55 and 56. They are quite short. Article 55 reads as follows:
With a view to the creation of conditions of stability and well-being which are necessary for peaceful and friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and selfdetermination of peoples, the United Nations shall promote:
a.	higher standards of living, full employment, and conditions of economic and social progress and development:
b.	solutions of international economic, social, health, and related problems; and international cultural and educational cooperation; and
c.	universal respect for, and observance of, human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion.
And article 56 contains this sentence:
All members pledge themselves to take joint and separate action in cooperation with the organization for the achievement of the purposes set forth in article 55.
We have formally assumed these obligations, or the government has assumed them cn behalf of our country. We have all approved them, and however much we may be inclined from time to time to forget them, they are there, they are staring us in the face, and I suggest that if we neglect them we shall do so at our peril.
I would like to read a few paragraphs from a pamphlet I have here entitled "Stories of Technical Assistance". The paragraph I wish to read was written by Mr. David Owen, executive chairman, technical assistance board. Then I would like to read some rather astonishing figures bringing to your attention the situation of a country which has not been favoured as has our own, because the contrast is so dramatic.
United Nations
First of all, from page 1 of "Stories of Technical Assistance" by Mr. Owen:
At the beginning of 1952, I made a journey that could only have been made in this century. It was a long journey, about 8,000 air miles, from Geneva to Indonesia and back. But it was also an absurdly short journey, for I visited Lebanon, India, Ceylon, Burma and Thailand, and yet had returned to Geneva about 30 days after I set out. This in itself would have bewildered the imagination of a Marco Polo. But what is more revealing is that few people today would feel anything surprising about such a journey. Marco Polo's wanderings through Asia amazed his contemporaries to the point of incredulity, and they had an important influence on firing the zest of renaissance man for venturing to the corners of the world. My own journey, as a feat of transportation, amazes no one, but what amazed me and ought surely to amaze others is the disparity between the kinds of development for which mankind is responsible. For though I, as a 20th century man, was travelling about Asia at a speed inconceivable to Marco Polo, I was looking at a world in which many of the human skills and social customs that he described 700 years ago have barely changed at all. To a remarkable degree we were visiting the same human landscape.
Having said that I want to quote a word from page 39 of this same pamphlet in regard to Libya, which we heard so much about recently. I wish to draw attention particularly to the extraordinarily low economic condition of that country. At the beginning of the Christian era that country was one of the granaries of the world, but it has been allowed to deteriorate. Although governmental services are on a very modest level, it is very doubtful whether Libya can keep up even its present standards. The pamphlet goes on to say:
Thus the Libyan economy cannot maintain even the present low standard of living, which averages in income per capita not much more than $30 a year.
I mention that to try to underline in our own minds the almost tragic contrast we find. If we are going to win this battle for men's minds it is perfectly obvious that we have to take a long view, and that we have to render assistance.
I am not going into the details. The minister has given us a good deal of information in that regard. All I wish to do is express my own view that this is a matter which we should all be regarding as of absolutely primary importance to us all, and that we should take a long and broad view. If we are to win it must be in the long run by convincing the nations of Asia that, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said, we are treating them as equals.
In that connection I should like to close these few remarks by reading briefly from the communique issued at the close of the conference in Australia the other day. Hon. members will recall that in the Colombo plan we

in the commonwealth have been showing our recognition of the need of assisting nations in the commonwealth who have been less favoured than some of the rest of us, and I wish to read part of the concluding words of the communique, which indeed seemed to me one of the most happily expressed and impressive political documents that I have read for some time.
